fields.hook:
Ten games to make you smarter, but more niche each time.
1.⁠ ⁠Chess. You already know this one, but basically it's a constant game of thinking several moves ahead and trying to predict what the other person will do.
2.⁠ ⁠Matiks. These are quick games of math, logic, and memory where you have to think against the clock. It's a good way to make your brain retrieve information quickly instead of sitting there thinking for ages.
3.⁠ ⁠Set. Here you have to identify patterns among different shapes, colors, and numbers. And the weird thing is, once your brain gets the hang of it, it starts seeing the patterns almost instantly.
4.⁠ ⁠Hive. It's like playing chess, but without a board. Each piece moves differently, and since there's no fixed grid, you have to constantly visualize what's happening.
5.⁠ ⁠Hanabi. You can see everyone else's cards except your own, so you have to communicate strategically without revealing too much information.
6.⁠ ⁠The Resistance. Basically, it's a social deduction game. The interesting part is trying to figure out who's lying based on incomplete information.

fields.hook:
Things you can do to develop a photographic memory. Please be careful because this can put a lot of strain on your brain. And stay till the third point because it's the most important.

First, we have Kim's Game. Look at a bunch of random objects for 30 seconds, cover them up, and try to recall every single one. This helps train your visual recall.

Next, we have the Leitner System. Use flashcards and move them into different boxes depending on how well you remember them. This helps you focus on what you're actually forgetting.

And last, we have playing Matiks. It's basically a brain exercise where you challenge yourself with quick math games, memory challenges, and logic puzzles against random opponents. fields.note:
10 out of 10 games to make you smart again, but they get progressively more niche.

Chess. You already know this one, but it's basically a constant exercise in planning several moves ahead and predicting what another person will do.

Matiks. Fast math, logic, and memory games where you have to think under a time limit. It's a good way to make your brain retrieve information quickly instead of letting you sit there thinking forever.

Set. You have to identify patterns across different shapes, colors, and numbers. The weird part is that once your brain gets it, you'll start seeing patterns almost instantly.

Hive. It's like chess without a board. Every piece moves differently, and because there's no fixed grid, you have to constantly visualize what's happening.

Hanabi. You can see everyone else's cards but not your own. You have to communicate strategically without giving away too much information.

The Resistance. It's basically social deduction, but the interesting part is trying to figure out who's lying based on incomplete information.

Quarto. Four different attributes, one winning line, and your opponent chooses the piece you have to play. So now you're solving the board while also thinking about what your opponent wants you to play.

Go. The rules are incredibly simple. The strategy is basically the opposite. You can spend years playing it and still keep discovering new patterns.

Follow for more ways to make yourself smarter.

fields.note:
this week
Things you can do to develop a photographic memory. Please be careful because this can put a lot of strain on your brain. And stay till the third point because it's the most important.

First, we have Kim's Game. Look at a bunch of random objects for 30 seconds, cover them up, and try to recall every single one. This helps train your visual recall.

Next, we have the Leitner System. Use flashcards and move them into different boxes depending on how well you remember them. This helps you focus on what you're actually forgetting.

And last, we have playing Matiks. It's basically a brain exercise where you challenge yourself with quick math games, memory challenges, and logic puzzles against random opponents. You can play these games on your phone to train your thinking and problem-solving skills instead of mindlessly scrolling.

Follow for more ways to keep your brain sharp!

fields.hook:
This is what how many times you six seven a day says about you.  

If you are six sevening one to five times a day, you're probably around 18 to 25. You're kind of into brain rot, but you don't know it that well. You probably reference triple T a few times a day, and maybe if you're lucky, you know Ballerina Cappuccino.

Now, if you're six sevening six to seven times a day, you're probably between the ages of 13 and 17. At this point, you'll probably be six sevening for the rest of your life. It has been engraved in your adolescent mind, and you are also chronically online. You probably know every single reference that has ever been on the internet, only starting from like 2020 though. You probably were one of the few that understood knee surgery tomorrow. Probably enjoy making fruit brain rot in your free time.

Now, if you're six sevening eight to 20 times per day, that means it's getting really bad. It's probably the only internet reference that you know, so that's why you keep repeating it. You're either under 10 years old or you're over 30. You probably know six seven in every language, but you actually don't know what it means and you don't even know who LaMelo is.

At this point, if you're in the age group that's over 30 that's six sevening eight to 20 times per day, you need help. Don't worry, I can support you. Just go to ultimatebrainrotmeter.com . take a test to check how cooked your brain is form brain rot, it will also curate a personalized prescription for you that’ll help you rehab

fields.hook:
Ten games to make you smarter, but more niche each time.
1.⁠ ⁠Chess. You already know this one, but basically it's a constant game of thinking several moves ahead and trying to predict what the other person will do.
2.⁠ ⁠Matiks. These are quick games of math, logic, and memory where you have to think against the clock. It's a good way to make your brain retrieve information quickly instead of sitting there thinking for ages.
3.⁠ ⁠Set. Here you have to identify patterns among different shapes, colors, and numbers. And the weird thing is, once your brain gets the hang of it, it starts seeing the patterns almost instantly.
4.⁠ ⁠Hive. It's like playing chess, but without a board. Each piece moves differently, and since there's no fixed grid, you have to constantly visualize what's happening.
5.⁠ ⁠Hanabi. You can see everyone else's cards except your own, so you have to communicate strategically without revealing too much information.
6.⁠ ⁠The Resistance. Basically, it's a social deduction game. The interesting part is trying to figure out who's lying based on incomplete information.

Set. You have to identify patterns across different shapes, colors, and numbers. The weird part is that once your brain gets it, you'll start seeing patterns almost instantly.

Hive. It's like chess without a board. Every piece moves differently, and because there's no fixed grid, you have to constantly visualize what's happening.

Hanabi. You can see everyone else's cards but not your own. You have to communicate strategically without giving away too much information.

The Resistance. It's basically social deduction, but the interesting part is trying to figure out who's lying based on incomplete information.

Quarto. Four different attributes, one winning line, and your opponent chooses the piece you have to play. So now you're solving the board while also thinking about what your opponent wants you to play.

Go. The rules are incredibly simple. The strategy is basically the opposite. You can spend years playing it and still keep discovering new patterns.

There’s never been a better time to become a polymath — someone who can learn across different fields and connect ideas others miss.

So how do you become one?

First, connect new information to what you already know. Whenever you learn something, ask: “What does this remind me of?” Your brain remembers things better through associations.

Second, interleave your learning. Don’t study one thing for three hours straight. Mix it up — read for an hour, listen to something, then solve problems or switch to a completely different type of task.

Third, train your brain deliberately. Spend a few minutes on Matiks playing math, logic, and memory games. It keeps you actively thinking instead of just consuming information.

And fourth, teach what you learn. Explain it to someone else in simple words. If you can't explain it simply, you probably haven't understood it deeply yet.

Learn broadly. Connect everything. Train your brain. Teach what you know.

That’s how you become a polymath.

"This is how I've been training my brain to become disgustingly articulate as a 22-year-old who's trying to decrease my dependence on AI for thinking.

1. Explaining what I've learnt out loud because understanding something and articulating it clearly are two different skills.

2. Playing brain games like Matiks. Here on Matiks, I practise mental maths, Sudoku, and logical reasoning through quick games instead of mindlessly scrolling.

3. Reading more and writing my own thoughts before asking AI to explain something, so I practise putting ideas into words myself.

The goal isn't to stop using AI. It's to make sure I'm still doing the thinking myself."

fields.hook:
Ten games to make you smarter, but more niche each time.
1.⁠ ⁠Chess. You already know this one, but basically it's a constant game of thinking several moves ahead and trying to predict what the other person will do.
2.⁠ ⁠Matiks. These are quick games of math, logic, and memory where you have to think against the clock. It's a good way to make your brain retrieve information quickly instead of sitting there thinking for ages.
3.⁠ ⁠Set. Here you have to identify patterns among different shapes, colors, and numbers. And the weird thing is, once your brain gets the hang of it, it starts seeing the patterns almost instantly.
4.⁠ ⁠Hive. It's like playing chess, but without a board. Each piece moves differently, and since there's no fixed grid, you have to constantly visualize what's happening.
5.⁠ ⁠Hanabi. You can see everyone else's cards except your own, so you have to communicate strategically without revealing too much information.
6.⁠ ⁠The Resistance. Basically, it's a social deduction game. The interesting part is trying to figure out who's lying based on incomplete information.

6/9 jasminegmuller - 2:51, 4.5M views, apr 12. "smart girl scroll" media-recommendation format.

"if you want to be a baddie, you need to be smart. i am going to help you derot your brain. i have put together a bunch of media pairings for you to have a smart girl scroll. my first recommendation is a podcast. it is the salem witch trial three-part series on the journey through time podcast. it's a lesson in history, but it's also a lesson in misogyny and hysteria and racism. i personally really struggle with remembering dates, specifically like history dates. numbers just don't like sink into my brain as easily as words do. listening to podcasts that have really interesting stories of specific time periods, it really helps me solidify like different time periods in my mind and understand like all the different phases of civilization and humanity. my next piece of media that i can recommend is something to read. i am addicted to substack. guys, if you are not on substack, get on that app. it is like twitter but for smart people. i'm literally obsessed with it. so i have one creative option and i have one educational option. for the educational option, i would recommend reading anti-intellectualism has a hidden target. talks about the rise of anti-intellectualism and how it coincidentally syncs up with the fact that women are making up most of the graduates in high-income countries. women have flipped the education gap. coincidentally, education is starting to become less and less valuable in society, which is why i'm saying real baddies are smart. and for my creative girlies, i would recommend reading why do people act like they have tomorrow to love you? i have read this article so many times this month because for some reason it's just really ringing true to me. it really speaks to the yearner in me and i feel like as women we have this ability to just romanticize everything and really look forward to the now. i don't think that that really goes hand in hand with society in the sense that society always makes us live for tomorrow. it always makes us live for the end goal rather than just being here right now and seizing the day. when you think of this concept in relation to love and relationships, i think it's so interesting. and the author of this article just wrote it so perfectly. it's one of those pieces that i just wish i had written like wow. for my girlies who want something visual, my film recommendation of the month is all we imagine as light. i actually watched it when it came out. it's such a beautiful and intimate film about three nurses who are working in mumbai. it's an indian drama and it's just filmed in a very nostalgic, beautiful, feminine way. it explores themes of friendship and loneliness, but i just loved the feeling of the film. my last recommendation is someone for you to follow. i love earthling ed's page. he is a vegan activist but also an author and the way that he speaks about animal cruelty and the intersectionality of most forms of activism and the way that we view animals and the way that we treat animals. i especially love conversations around um gendered violence within animal farming. but yeah, honeys, we need to get smart. we're outsmarting the men and i love to see it. anti-intellectualism is on the rise. no brain rot around here. love you."

fields.hook:
Things you can do to develop a photographic memory. Please be careful because this can put a lot of strain on your brain. And stay till the third point because it's the most important.

First, we have Kim's Game. Look at a bunch of random objects for 30 seconds, cover them up, and try to recall every single one. This helps train your visual recall.

Next, we have the Leitner System. Use flashcards and move them into different boxes depending on how well you remember them. This helps you focus on what you're actually forgetting.

And last, we have playing Matiks. It's basically a brain exercise where you challenge yourself with quick math games, memory challenges, and logic puzzles against random opponents. You can play these games on your phone to train your thinking and problem-solving skills instead of mindlessly scrolling.

Follow for more ways to keep your brain sharp!
